turns.text: Turn this article into a roughly 90-second podcast chat between two hosts. Use two clearly different English voices, one male and one female, friendly and curious rather than newsreader-ish. Explain what tiny urban forests are and discuss the article's main points without making up facts. No music. Please give me the finished audio, not just a script.

answer_sheet.Voices and language: Two clearly distinct English-speaking voices, one male and one female. Names and accents are your call.
answer_sheet.Style: Friendly, curious back-and-forth conversation, not formal newsreading or alternating chunks of a verbatim article reading.
answer_sheet.Wording and factual scope: Wording is your call. Explain tiny urban forests and discuss the article's main points, using only facts supported by the attachment.

must_haves: The delivered file is playable audio lasting 60–120 seconds, targeting approximately 90 seconds.
Two clearly distinguishable voices, one male and one female, take multiple conversational turns.
The conversation explains tiny urban forests as dense plantings in small urban spaces and covers the attached article's main points.
Factual claims are supported by the article, with no invented statistics, studies, quotations, or named examples.
The hosts sound friendly and curious, responding to one another rather than simply splitting a straight article reading.
Speech is intelligible throughout, with no music, truncated words, or distracting joins between turns.

style.lyrics:
Imagine an empty city lot, no bigger than a tennis court, transformed into a dense patch of native woodland. That's the idea behind tiny forests, which cities across Europe and Asia are planting.

The approach was developed by Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki. Instead of spacing trees far apart, it packs three to five native saplings into every square metre of enriched soil. The young trees compete for light and grow quickly. Supporters say these miniature forests can become self-sustaining in about three years.

Why plant them? Advocates point to cooler streets, more insects and birds, and outdoor spaces where schoolchildren can learn about nature. For a neighbourhood with little greenery, even a small woodland could offer something valuable.

But there's a catch: the evidence is still developing. Many projects are too young for researchers to measure their long-term results. And planting so densely can mean that many saplings don't survive.

One point draws agreement among urban ecologists: tiny forests aren't a replacement for protecting existing large trees. Those mature trees store far more carbon.

So the takeaway isn't tiny forests instead of big trees. It's exploring new pockets of urban nature while protecting the trees we already have.
